resources.title: States of Matter

content.topicNotes: States of Matter There are 3 different states of matter. Solids A solid has a fixed shape because of the strong forces between its particles. Solids cannot be compressed because their particles are already very close together and cannot flow. The particles in a solid are arranged in an ordered pattern. The particles in a solid move around a fixed point. Liquids Liquids cannot be compressed because their particles are already very close together. In a liquid, the particles are in contact with one another, but they can still move. This allows a liquid to flow and take the shape of its container. Particles in a liquid are arranged in a disordered pattern. Gases Gases can be compressed because their particles are very far apart. When water evaporates to become steam (gas), its volume increases by 1000x. The particles in a gas are free to move in any direction. Because of this, a gas can flow, has no fixed shape and completely fills its container. The particles in a gas move randomly and are not organised in any way. Properties of Solids, Liquids and Gases The behaviour of solids, liquids and gases can be explained by considering the forces, distances, and motion of particles. Solids Particles are very close together and arranged in a fixed, regular structure. Strong forces of attraction hold them in place. Particles vibrate about fixed positions but cannot move freely. This gives solids a definite shape and volume. Liquids Particles are close together but arranged more irregularly. Forces of attraction are weaker than in solids, so particles can slide past each other. This allows liquids to flow and take the shape of their container, while still keeping a fixed volume. Gases Particles are far apart compared with their size. Forces between particles are very weak (almost negligible). Particles move freely and rapidly in all directions. Gases therefore have no fixed shape or volume and can be compressed easily. States of Matter - Examples There are 3 states of matter: solid, liquid and gas. 3 states of matter Red screen: atoms in a solid. Blue screen: atoms in a liquid. Yellow screen: atoms in a gas.

resources.title: The Big Bang

content.topicNotes: The Big Bang The Big Bang theory says that the universe began from a single point. The Big Bang The universe began from a very small region that was hot and dense. This region ‘exploded’ and started expanding. This expansion is still happening. Evidence There are many forms of evidence to support the Big Bang model of the universe. An example is the observation of red-shift in distant galaxies. This suggests that the universe has expanded from a single point and continues to expand today. The Big Bang The universe began from a very small region that was hot and dense. This region ‘exploded’ and started expanding. This expansion is still happening. The Big Bang Because the sun is also moving, this is how our solar system looks: Gaps in Knowledge Although science can explain so much of what we see in the universe, there is still a lot we cannot currently explain. How expansion happens Scientists still don’t understand everything about the universe. They don’t understand much about how the universe is expanding. Dark matter and dark energy Some scientists think that the universe is mostly made up of dark matter (an unknown substance that holds galaxies together but doesn’t emit electromagnetic radiation) and dark energy (the thing that causes the universe to quickly expand). But no one really knows what these are - they are just theories. The Universe Scientists don't know everything about the universe. Some scientists think that the universe is mostly made up of dark matter (an unknown substance that holds galaxies together but doesn’t emit electromagnetic radiation) and dark energy (the thing that causes the universe to quickly expand).

resources.title: The Earth

content.topicNotes: The Earth Basic facts The Earth is a planet. The Earth spins on its axis. The axis is tilted. The Earth makes one full spin in about 24 hours. Apparent daily motion of the Sun The spinning of the Earth around its axis causes the Sun to appear to move across the sky each day. We call this the apparent daily motion of the Sun. Day and night When our part of Earth faces the Sun, we see daylight. When our part of Earth faces away from the Sun, we see night. The tilt of the axis affects how long days and nights last in different seasons. This cycle of day and night repeats every 24 hours. Apparent Daily Motion of the Sun The spinning of the Earth around its axis causes the Sun to appear to move across the sky each day. We call this the apparent daily motion of the Sun. The Earth's orbit around the Sun The orbit The Earth moves around the Sun. This movement is called an orbit. The Earth takes about 365 days to complete one orbit. Seasons The orbit of the Earth around the Sun causes the seasons to repeat every year. The tilt of the Earth’s axis changes how sunlight falls on different parts of the Earth. This is why we see summer, autumn, winter, and spring. Orbital speed We can calculate the Earth’s average orbital speed. The formula is $$v = \dfrac{2πr}{T}$$. $$r$$ is the average radius of the orbit. $$T$$ is the time the Earth takes for one orbit.

resources.title: The Hubble Constant

content.topicNotes: The Hubble Constant The Hubble Constant The Hubble constant (H0) links a galaxy’s speed and distance. It is defined as the ratio of the speed at which the galaxy is moving away from the Earth to its distance from the Earth. Current estimate The formula to calculate it is $$H_0 = \dfrac{d}{v}$$ $$v$$ is the speed the galaxy is moving away (m/s) $$d$$ is the distance of the galaxy (m) The current estimate of the Hubble constant is about 2.2 × 10-18 per second. The age of the Universe The equation $$\dfrac{d}{v} = \dfrac{1}{H_0}$$ represents an estimate for the age of the Universe. This suggests that, if galaxies are moving apart now, they must once have been much closer together. This is strong evidence that all matter in the Universe was once at a single point, which is the idea behind the Big Bang theory.

resources.title: The Solar System & The Accretion Model

content.topicNotes: The Solar System Our solar system is a small part of the Milky Way Galaxy. It is made up of: The Sun The Sun is the only star in our solar system. Planets and dwarf planets Planets and dwarf planets orbit around the Sun. There are eight planets in our solar system (Pluto is a dwarf planet). Moons Moons are in orbit around many of the planets. Moons are called natural satellites. Comets and asteroids Comets and asteroids also orbit around the Sun. Planets in the Solar System There are eight planets in our solar system: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune (Pluto is a dwarf planet). Jupiter Earth Saturn The Accretion Model Characteristics of the planets The four inner planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars) are small and rocky. The four outer planets (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune) are large and gaseous. The accretion model Billions of years ago, the Solar System began as a huge cloud of gas and dust (called a nebula) in space. The cloud contained many different elements, such as hydrogen, helium, carbon, oxygen, and iron. Slowly, gravity began pulling the gas and dust particles closer. As particles collided, they stuck together, forming bigger and bigger clumps. As gravity pulled the cloud inward, it started to rotate. This rotation caused the cloud to flatten into a thin, spinning accretion disc with most material near the centre. Formation of the Sun and planets Most of the material moved to the centre of the disc, where gravity made it collapse and heat up. This eventually formed the Sun. Smaller clumps of dust and rock in the disc collided and stuck together. These growing bodies are called planetesimals. Over time, they grew larger, becoming the planets. Why are planets different? Close to the Sun: It was very hot, so gases like hydrogen and helium escaped. Only heavy, solid materials stayed, forming the small, rocky inner planets. Far from the Sun: It was cooler, so gases could stay. Planets here gathered huge amounts of gas around a rocky core, becoming the large, gaseous outer planets.
content.description: Physics: Cambridge International GCSE Supplement > Space Physics > The Earth & the Solar System

resources.title: The Sun as a Star

content.topicNotes: The Sun The Sun was formed from a cloud of dust and gas (called a nebula). The forces of gravity pulled the dust and gas together. Cloud of gas and dust The gas and dust collapsed. The cloud suddenly decreased in volume as the pressure in the cloud increased. This formed a protostar. Main sequence Materials continued to collide (come together) until the temperature and pressure were high enough for hydrogen nuclei to start fusing and form helium (in nuclear fusion). The star then went into a stable period, called a ‘main star sequence’. Nuclear fusion The energy released from the nuclear fusion in the Sun keeps the Sun’s core hot. Stable The Sun is still in its stable main sequence phase. In this phase, the outward force of the energy released by nuclear fusion is balanced by the force of gravity pulling the Sun inwards. The Sun The Sun is the only star in our solar system. The energy released from the nuclear fusion in the Sun keeps the Sun’s core hot.
content.description: Physics: Cambridge International GCSE Supplement > Space Physics > Stars & the Universe

resources.title: The Sun's Gravitational Field

content.topicNotes: The Sun's Gravitational Field (cont.) Effect on the planets The Sun’s gravitational field strength decreases as you move further away. Planets closer to the Sun move faster in their orbits. Planets further away move more slowly. Orbits Orbits are often elliptical (oval-shaped), not perfect circles. An object in an elliptical orbit travels faster when closer to the Sun. This happens because of the conservation of energy. Conservation of energy Near the Sun, the object is deeper in the gravitational field, so gravitational potential energy decreases. This energy changes into kinetic energy, so the object speeds up. Further from the Sun, the opposite happens: more potential energy, less kinetic energy, so the object slows down.
content.description: Physics: Cambridge International GCSE Supplement > Space Physics > The Earth & the Solar System

resources.title: Thermal Expansion

content.topicNotes: Thermal Expansion All materials expand when they are heated. This is called thermal expansion. In solids The molecules in a solid are fixed. When the temperature rises, the molecules vibrate more and are pushed apart. Engineers leave gaps in train tracks to allow for thermal expansion. These gaps create the “clickety-click” sound that trains make. Engineers also allow for thermal expansion when designing buildings and bridges. In liquids When heated, the molecules in a liquid move faster and are pushed apart (like in solids). For a 1°C rise in temperature, a liquid will expand more than a solid. In gases When heated, molecules in a gas will move faster. For a 1°C rise in temperature, the volume of a gas will increase more than the volume of a liquid. If a gas is in a fixed container, its volume cannot change. Both the force exerted on the container walls and the pressure will rise. Examples Buildings and bridges need to be safe at all temperatures. Engineers need to allow for thermal expansion and often use steel reinforcement to strengthen buildings. The “clickety-click” sound of trains is produced by small gaps between the train tracks. These gaps exist to allow for thermal expansion. Thomas the Tank Engine Thomas the Tank Engine uses Physics to his advantage every day. Thermal Expansion The “clickety-click” sound of trains is produced by small gaps between the train tracks. These gaps are designed to leave room for thermal expansion. Friction The friction between a train and the tracks will act against the direction of the train's motion (movement). Momentum Gordon (the tank engine) is heavier and faster than Thomas (the tank engine), so Gordon will have more momentum.

resources.title: Thin Converging Lenses 1

content.topicNotes: Thin Converging Lenses A thin converging lens (curved piece of glass) causes parallel rays of light that pass through it to converge (come together). Refraction When a beam of light strikes a thin converging lens, the light is refracted twice: Once towards the normal (90 degrees to the lens) as the light enters the lens; And once away from the normal (90 degrees to the lens) as the light leaves the lens. Note: It is assumed that the lens is very thin to only consider one reflection at the optical axis. When you see ray diagrams the lens will be represented by a single line. Optical axis The optical axis is the line perpendicular to the principal axis and passing through the optical centre (lens’ centre). It is used to show the position of the lens. Principal focus Light rays that are parallel to the optical axis pass through the lens and converge (come together) at the principal focus. There is one principal focus on each side of the lens as light can pass through the lens in either direction. Focal length The focal length is the distance from the centre of the lens to the principal focus. Thin Converging Lenses - Example A thin converging lens (curved piece of glass) causes parallel rays of light that pass through it to converge (come together). resources.title: Three Types of Emission

content.topicNotes: Three Types of Nuclear Emission Alpha, beta and gamma radiation all have different properties. Alpha radiation Each alpha particle contains two protons and two neutrons. Because of this, alpha particles have a relative mass of 4. Because the particles are big and heavy, alpha radiation is strongly ionising. It does a lot of damage, but is stopped by a small amount of matter (like paper). Beta radiation Beta radiation is made up of high-energy electrons. Beta radiation is more ionising than gamma radiation, but less ionising than alpha radiation. It can pass through paper, but is stopped by aluminium foil. Gamma radiation Gamma radiation is weakly ionising. It does less damage than beta or alpha radiation, but it is stopped only by centimetres of lead or concrete.

content.topicNotes: Transformer Equation The potential difference across the primary coil (Vp) divided by potential difference across the secondary coil (Vs) is equal to the number of turns on the primary coil (Np) divided by the number of turns on the secondary coil (Ns). Equation If there are four times as many turns on the secondary coil as on the primary coil, then the voltage output on the secondary coil will be four times the input voltage.

resources.title: Transverse Wave

content.topicNotes: Transverse Waves Here are some examples of transverse waves: Moving springs Waving/moving the coils of a spring will make the coils move up and down as the wave passes. They then return to their original position after the wave has passed. This shows that a wave moves without transferring matter because the spring coils do not travel along with the wave. Mexican wave A “Mexican wave” at a sports event is an example of a transverse wave. The wave spreads around the stadium as the people stand up and sit down one after the other (at right angles to the direction of the people’s motion). Corks bobbing A cork bobbing on the water shows how a transverse wave works. Transverse Waves - Examples A “Mexican wave” at a sports event is an example of a transverse wave. resources.title: Triangular Prisms 1

content.topicNotes: Triangular Prisms A triangular prism can also be used to create a spectrum. Different frequencies travel at different speeds The incident ray of white light enters the prism. The different frequencies of the colours travel at different speeds through the prism. Different colours are refracted by different amounts The different colours (frequencies) are refracted by a different amount when they enter the prism. Therefore, the emergent ray (coming out of the medium) is red on one side and violet on the other. Different speeds of light Red light’s speed changes the least when entering the prism, so its direction changes the least. Violet light’s speed changes the most (slows down) in the prism, so its direction changes the most. Triangular Prisms - Example A triangular prism can also be used to create a spectrum. resources.title: Turning Effect

content.topicNotes: Turning Effect A moment is the turning effect of a force around a fixed point. Doors Doors open more easily if we press (exert force) far away from the hinge, rather than next to the hinge. Pushing further away from the hinge (fixed point) means the moment is larger. See-saw Balancing on a see-saw is a good example for demonstrating how turning effects work. To balance the weight of a heavier person, a lighter person must sit further away from the pivot. Wrench When a mechanic uses a long wrench to tighten or loosen bolts, such as those holding a car wheel in place, they will always hold it at the furthest end from the bolt. This uses the turning effect to magnify the force of their hand on the wrench.

resources.title: Types of Transformer

content.topicNotes: Step-Up and Step-Down Transformers Transformers are separated into step-up transformers and step-down transformers. Step-up transformer Ns > Np . The secondary coil has more turns than primary coil. The potential difference across the secondary coil is greater than the potential difference across the primary coil. (The potential difference is ‘stepped up’.) Step-down transformer Ns < Np . The secondary coil has fewer turns than primary coil. The potential difference across the secondary coil is less than the potential difference across the primary coil. (The potential difference is ‘stepped down’.) Step-Up and Step-Down Transformers Transformers are separated into step-up transformers and step-down transformers. Step-up transformer Ns > Np. The secondary coil has more turns than primary coil. The potential difference across the secondary coil is greater than the potential difference across the primary coil. (The potential difference is ‘stepped up’.) Step-down transformer Ns < Np. The secondary coil has fewer turns than primary coil. The potential difference across the secondary coil is less than the potential difference across the primary coil. (The potential difference is ‘stepped down’.)

resources.title: Uses of Energy Transfer

content.topicNotes: Uses of Energy Transfer Conduction, convection, and radiation are used a lot in everyday life. Solar panels The solar panels that generate electricity are dark so that they can absorb the maximum amount of the sunlight hitting them. Radiators Radiators are used for heating. A radiator’s primary way of heating a room is actually convection. If the primary way was radiation, then they should be painted black, as this is the colour that best emits radiation. Vacuum flasks A vacuum flask keeps drinks hot or cold. Outside of the container, there is a vacuum layer (with no air in) surrounded by walls lined with silver. This reduces the heat transferred to the surroundings. The silvered walls are good reflectors and poor emitters of heat. This also reduces the heat transferred by radiation. Heating in the kitchen pans Heat from the cooker is transferred to the pan by conduction (if on a hot plate) or by radiation/convection (if gas flame). The pan, usually made of metal, conducts heat quickly to the food. Energy is transferred from the hot surface of the pan to the cooler food, cooking it. Fire burning wood or coal Energy stored chemically in the fuel is released as heat and light during combustion. Heat is transferred to the surroundings by infrared radiation, which can travel through air. Convection currents also carry warm air upwards, heating the room. Radiator in a car The radiator transfers heat away from the engine to stop it from overheating. Hot coolant fluid from the engine passes through thin metal pipes in the radiator. Heat is transferred to the outside air by conduction (through the metal), convection (air moving past the radiator), and radiation (infrared emitted from the hot surface). Santorini - White Houses Santorini is a place in Greece, where it is very hot. Lots of the houses are white because, white is a good reflector of infra-red radiation in the day. At night, not much heat is emitted because white is a bad emitter of radiation. White houses

resources.title: Uses of Magnets & Currents

content.topicNotes: Electromagnets - Uses of Magnets & Currents An electromagnet is formed when a current carrying wire is wrapped around an iron core. The iron core makes the magnetic field caused by the current flowing through the wire stronger. Electromagnets can be used in a number of ways. Scrap yards In scrap yards, to lift and move magnetic metals from one place to another. Washing machines To lock washing machine doors during a cycle. Magnetic Effect of a Current in Relays and Loudspeakers Relays When current flows through a coil of wire in a relay, it produces a magnetic field that magnetises an iron armature. The armature is pulled towards the electromagnet, which operates a switch in another circuit. This allows a low current circuit (e.g. a control circuit) to switch on a high current circuit (e.g. a motor). Applications: Car starter motors, central heating systems, and remote-control switching. Loudspeakers In a loudspeaker, a coil of wire is placed in a strong permanent magnetic field. When an alternating current (AC) passes through the coil, the current produces a magnetic field that interacts with the permanent magnet. This causes the coil (and the attached diaphragm/cone) to vibrate back and forth, producing sound waves. Applications: Radios, televisions, mobile phones, and music speakers.
content.description: Physics: Cambridge International GCSE Supplement > Electricity & Magnetism > Force on a Current-Carrying Conductor

resources.title: Variable Resistance

content.topicNotes: Wires and Resistance The resistance of a wire depends on the wire’s length and cross-sectional area of the circular end of the wire. Resistance (in ohms) is proportional to (α) the length (in metres) divided by the cross-sectional area (in metres squared). Size of a wire Increasing the length of a wire, increases the resistance of the wire. Decreasing the cross-sectional area of the wire increases its resistance. So short, wide wires have less resistance than long, narrow wires. Wire thickness The cross-sectional area (A) of a circular wire is equal to π times its radius (r) squared. Therefore, doubling the thickness of a wire quadruples its cross-sectional area. Wires and Resistance - Example The resistance of a wire depends on the wire’s length and the cross-sectional area of the circular end of the wire. Resistance Resistance (in ohms) is proportional to the length of the wire (in metres) divided by cross-sectional area (in metres squared).

content.topicNotes: Velocity vs Speed Velocity and speed are not the same thing. Speed Speed is a scalar quantity. Scalar quantities only have a magnitude (size). Scalar quantities, like speed, do not have a direction. Velocity Velocity describes an object’s direction as well as its speed. Velocity is a vector quantity because it has a magnitude (or size) and a direction. Velocity - Examples Velocity describes an object’s direction as well as its speed. resources.title: Water Energy

content.topicNotes: Water (Hydroelectric Power) Water high above the ground is a store of gravitational potential energy. Hydroelectric dams trap water and allowing it to fall rotates a turbine, which turns a generator. Advantages Renewable. More reliable than wind and solar. Disadvantages Hydroelectric dams often change the paths of rivers, which can move people out of houses and harm local wildlife. Energy Step 1 In a hydroelectric power station, a reservoir is filled by rainfall and rivers. Water is stored above the turbines, giving it gravitational potential energy The dam then allows the water to fall, rotating a turbine This turbine turns, converting kinetic energy into electrical energy through a generator. Step 2 In a pumped storage system, water can be pumped back up to the reservoir at times of low demand. This stores energy that can be released when demand is high. Water (Hydroelectric Power) - Example Water high off the ground is a store of gravitational potential energy. Hydroelectric dams trap water and allowing it to fall rotates a turbine, which turns a generator. Hoover Dam The Hoover Dam in the USA generates energy using hydroelectric power.
